title: Founder Mode: why scaling advice to "hire good people and let them work" fails founders
summary: Graham argues there are two ways to run a company: founder mode and manager mode. Standard advice to hire good people and give them room is how to run a company you didn't found, and it damages founder-led companies. Founder mode breaks the rule that CEOs deal only with direct reports, and is still poorly understood.

principles.text: Conventional scaling advice is manager mode, written for professional managers, and it often damages founder-led companies.
principles.quote: what they were being told was how to run a company you hadn't founded — how to run a company if you're merely a professional manager. But this m.o. is so much less effective that to founders it feels broken.

principles.text: Scaling a startup does not have to mean switching to manager mode. Founders can do things managers can't.
principles.quote: There are things founders can do that managers can't, and not doing them feels wrong to founders, because it is.

principles.text: Treating org-chart subtrees as black boxes and avoiding details can let weak hires drive the company down.
principles.quote: hire good people and give them room to do their jobs. Sounds great when it's described that way, doesn't it? Except in practice, judging from the report of founder after founder, what this often turns out to mean is: hire professional fakers and let them drive the company into the ground.

principles.text: Founder mode breaks the rule that the CEO engages only through direct reports. Skip-level meetings become normal.
principles.quote: it's going to break the principle that the CEO should engage with the company only via his or her direct reports. "Skip-level" meetings will become the norm

principles.text: Founders can use unconventional mechanisms, like Jobs's retreat for the 100 most important people regardless of rank, to keep a big company feeling like a startup.
principles.quote: Steve Jobs used to run an annual retreat for what he considered the 100 most important people at Apple, and these were not the 100 people highest on the org chart.

principles.text: Delegation is still necessary at scale, and autonomy borders vary by company and over time as managers earn trust.
principles.quote: Obviously founders can't keep running a 2000 person company the way they ran it when it had 20. There's going to have to be some amount of delegation.
